title: United States v. Nova Scotia Food Products Corp. (1977)
shortTitle: United States v. Nova Scotia Food Products Corp. (1977)
summary: The FDA’s undisclosed scientific basis and unanswered material objections made its smoked-whitefish rule invalid as applied in an enforcement action.

sections.Parties: The United States sought to enforce FDA fish-processing regulations against Nova Scotia Food Products and other appellants. An industry organization intervened in the challenge to the rule’s application.
sections.Material Facts: The FDA required specified time, temperature, and salinity conditions to control botulism in smoked fish. Inspectors found that the appellants did not meet those parameters, and the processors did not dispute noncompliance. They argued that compliance would destroy a marketable whitefish product. Industry and another federal agency had proposed species-specific standards and alternative use of nitrite and salt. The FDA did not disclose the scientific studies it relied on during the comment period and did not meaningfully answer the feasibility and alternative-processing objections. The administrative record was assembled later from files and participants’ recollections.
sections.Procedural History: The district court, after a hearing, enjoined processing that failed to meet the regulation. The Second Circuit reviewed that enforcement judgment, not a direct petition for review of rulemaking. It rejected the statutory-authority challenge but held the regulation invalid as applied to the relevant whitefish processing. It could not use this appeal to remand the rulemaking for another comment round.
sections.Issue: Did notice-and-comment procedure and the statement of basis and purpose adequately expose the FDA’s scientific rationale and address material comments? Could the processors instead introduce new scientific evidence at the enforcement trial to challenge the rule?
sections.Holding: The rule was procedurally defective and arbitrary as applied to non-vacuum-packed hot-smoked whitefish. Important scientific data should have been disclosed for comment, and the agency needed to address the significant feasibility and alternative-processing issues. The district court properly excluded the proposed new evidence on issues already presented to the agency; review of the rule proceeded on the administrative record.
sections.Reasoning:
Meaningful comment requires access to the important studies and methods supporting a technical proposal. Here those materials were collected by the agency and were not exposed for informed criticism. The court distinguished legitimate agency expertise from concealing available research whose applicability required examination. It also required a rational account of why uniform parameters fit diverse fish species.

The duty to provide reasons required attention to significant objections, including the possibility that the rule would eliminate the product commercially and that other preservatives could achieve safety at lower temperatures. Public health could justify even severe economic consequences, but the agency had to disclose whether it considered compliance feasible or chose safety despite infeasibility. The court did not decide scientific policy by comparing new trial evidence and did not demand formal adjudicatory findings. The procedural requirements served both participation and review of the rule’s rational basis.

topics.lrs-o-rulemaking-record: Undisclosed scientific premises and unanswered material objections prevented meaningful participation and adequate review of the processing rule.
topics.lrs-o-section-553: The court derived disclosure and a meaningful basis-and-purpose explanation from § 553 in informal rulemaking challenged through enforcement.
topics.lrs-n-hard-look: Nova Scotia's demand that the agency answer significant comments and disclose its data is a canonical hard-look application.
